title: Smallest Number After Dropping Digits
statement:
You get a non-negative integer written as a digit string num and a number k. Delete exactly k digits; the remaining digits keep their order. Return the smallest number you can get, as a string.

Write the result without leading zeros. If nothing is left, or only zeros are left, return "0".

examples.why: Drop the 5 (a bigger digit in front of a 2) and the 9 (a bigger digit in front of a 1).
Dropping the 3 leaves "0200". Leading zeros vanish, so this beats dropping a 0 ("3200" or "3020").
The digits only rise, so no digit is bigger than the one after it. Drop from the end.

constraints: num has only digits and no leading zeros, except "0" itself
hints: The first digit of the result matters most. When does dropping a digit make the number smaller?
If a digit is bigger than the one right after it, dropping it lowers that position. Dropping the first such digit is always a safe move.
Scan left to right with a stack. While k > 0 and the top of the stack is bigger than the current digit, pop it. If k is still positive at the end, pop from the back. Then strip leading zeros.

explain.intuition:
Numbers of the same length compare by their first different digit, so the left side matters most. Look at the first place where a digit is bigger than the next one, like the 5 before the 2 in "52914". Dropping it pulls a smaller digit into that position, and no other single deletion does better. If the digits only rise, the best deletion is the last digit.

Repeating that k times rescans the string each time. A stack does the same work in one pass: it holds the digits kept so far in non-decreasing order. Each new digit pops every bigger digit off the top while deletions remain, exactly like removing "a bigger digit before a smaller one" as soon as you see it.
steps: For each digit d: while k > 0 and the top is bigger than d, pop and decrease k. Then push d.
If k is still positive, pop k digits from the end; what remains is non-decreasing, so the end holds the biggest ones.
Join the stack, strip leading zeros, and return "0" if the result is empty.
pitfalls: Dropping the largest digits. In "4170" with k = 1, dropping the 7 gives 410, but dropping the 4 gives 170. Position matters more than size.
Forgetting the leftover deletions when the digits rise, like "123". The stack keeps everything and must be trimmed from the end.

solutions.title: Remove one peak at a time
solutions.idea: Repeat k times: delete the first digit that is bigger than its right neighbour, or the last digit if there is none.

solutions.title: Monotonic stack
solutions.idea: Keep the kept digits non-decreasing: each new digit pops bigger digits while deletions remain.

followups: Return the largest number instead. What changes?
Pick exactly k digits from two arrays, keeping each array's order, to build the largest number. How does the stack idea help?
